pages.name: Paying, the states, and the phone

artboards.title: Proposed — paying somebody, which is where prompt() used to be

annotations.text:
THE JOB OF THIS SCREEN

You settled four things, and everything here follows from them.

1. THE QUESTION IS "CAN I PAY THEM?" So the first figure on the screen is what is actually in the drawer, not what is owed. "You owe 1,627,000" is half a sentence on payday; the whole one is whether today's cash covers it, and if not, who is left over. This screen has never carried a cash figure at all.

2. YOU PAY ONE PERSON AT A TIME. So there is no batch pay run. Pay stays a per-row action — but it is a proper panel inside the open row, with the amount, the fortnight, the account and its balance all on screen, instead of the browser prompt() box the code opens today. Page 2 draws it.

3. RENT AND WAGES STAY ON ONE SCREEN, WAGES LEADING. Rent is two lines a month; it does not deserve a co-equal panel with its own table and its own oxide button. It becomes a two-row PREMISES block at the head of the same queue, in the same pay order. The agreements table itself moves behind a link in the rail — it is setup, not work.

4. ON THE PHONE YOU READ AND RECORD, YOU DO NOT PAY. A payment writes a Cash Book entry, and a mis-tap in a yard is a wrong ledger entry nobody finds until the day fails to reconcile. So the phone's one accent action is "Record a day somebody missed" — which is the thing that actually happens away from the desk.

Everything is drawn from index.html's own values: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, and the .ow-* console components already shipping on Today, Debtors, Creditors, Follow-ups, Pricing, Consignment and What's coming. No new colour, no new weight, no new type size, no fourteenth button family.

The figures are consistent with the real arithmetic: a 30-day wage month, a fortnight that is exactly half of it, a weekly rate of 105,000 costing 450,000 a month, absences deducted at the day rate, and a balance that floors at zero — which is why an overpayment can only be seen if the screen says so on purpose.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT AS IT STANDS →

1. A 190-CHARACTER PARAGRAPH IN THE PAGE HEAD, unmeasured, sitting open above the money. Every converted screen puts the name, one line and a hairline here, with the long version behind the "i".

2. THE HEADLINE FIGURE IS IN THE WRONG FACE. .age-pos-total b sets 1,627,000 in ARCHIVO BLACK at 34px. Archivo Black is loaded for page names only; money is IBM Plex Mono, tabular. 34px is not on the ramp either.

3. FIVE BORDERED TILES, AND NOT ONE OF THEM ANSWERS THE QUESTION. Cost, paid, wages, rent, days missed — an accounting summary of a month, on the screen you open to decide whether you can pay somebody on Friday. There is no cash figure anywhere on it. The tiles are also radius 10 with per-tile borders, where the system's strip is one bordered region with hairline dividers.

4. UP TO FIVE PROSE VERDICT BLOCKS, STACKED. Late, uncosted, no pay rate, overpaid, days missed — renderPayrollPosition can emit all five at once, and here four do. That is roughly 320px of coloured paragraphs between the figures and the list, two of them crimson, arguing with each other for the eye. Each is a real fact; none of them is a paragraph.

5. NINE COLUMNS, WITH AN <INPUT> IN ONE OF THEM. The days box is how a daily worker's month gets costed — the single most consequential typing on the screen — and it sits in a 76px cell in a table row with no label, no rate beside it and no total that moves.

6. "NONE" ON EVERY WAGE ROW. The missed-days button is drawn on all seven rows whether or not anybody was absent, so the column is mostly a word that means nothing repeated seven times.

7. SETTLED ROWS ARE DIMMED TO opacity:.62 — the whole row, figures included. A wage the shop has paid is not less true, and 62% grey on white puts the ink under the contrast floor.

8. PAY OPENS prompt(). A browser dialog, with the amount typed into an OS text box, followed by a second dialog asking which account. This is the act that writes to the Cash Book.

9. THE ORDER IS ALPHABETICAL BY KIND, THEN BY NAME. "rent" sorts before "wage", so the premises happen to come first — not because one of them is 26 days late. Nothing on the screen ranks by what to pay first, and nothing says how it is ordered.

10. THE STATE COLUMN REPEATS THE BALANCE COLUMN. Still owed 0 → "Paid". Still owed with a past date → "Late". The one state that is genuinely extra information — Overpaid — is a pill in the same tone as Not costed.

11. RENT IS A SECOND PANEL WITH A SECOND OXIDE BUTTON. "Add premises" is accent, and so is "Run this month's payroll" when it appears. The accent is meant to appear once per screen: it is the one thing to do next.

12. THE MONTH IS SAID TWICE AND NAVIGATED SIDEWAYS. The panel heading is rewritten to "August 2026" while a "This month" button sits beside it — and the month is the scope of the whole screen, not of one panel.

13. OFF-SYSTEM VALUES THROUGHOUT: sizes 10.5, 11.5, 12.5, 13.5, 34; radii 10, 12 and 999 where the system is 4/6/8; a drop shadow on every panel where depth in this app is hairlines.

THE PROPOSAL — what changed, and why

THE STRIP LEADS WITH WHAT IS IN THE DRAWER. Four questions and not one more: what you hold today and what share of the month it covers; what is still to pay, stated with how many months are settled and how many cannot be costed; what is ALREADY LATE, in crimson, because rent and wages are the two bills that cost more than money when they slip — the existing code's own sentence, kept; and what FALLS DUE ON THE 31st, in amber, because the whole payroll lands on one day and four days' notice is the difference between arranging it and being short. "In hand" is ink, not a state colour: money you hold is a fact.

THE COVER LINE. Rows are ranked by what to pay first and a dashed line across the list says how far today's cash reaches: the three above come to 1,250,000 of the 1,450,000 in hand; the two below need 377,000 against 200,000 left — 177,000 short before Monday. It states its own assumption (paying down the list in order, in full) in the same breath, so it reads as a measurement rather than as the app deciding who gets paid. Nothing below it is dimmed.

ONE QUEUE, TWO GROUPS, ONE ORDER. Premises first, then people, then — below the payable ones — the month that cannot be costed, then what is settled. The rule is written in the panel head and again in the rail: already late, then falls due soonest, then largest. A list that reorders itself without saying why is a list nobody trusts.

THE ROW CARRIES THE REASON IT IS WHERE IT IS. A third column between the name and the figure: "26 days late — was due 1 Aug" in crimson, "Due Mon 31 Aug — in 4 days" in ink, "Not costed — enter her days" in amber. The state pill is gone; so is the duplicate.

THE OPEN ROW IS THE MONTH, IN FULL. Days worked as a real labelled field with the rate and the arithmetic beside it — not a 76px box in a cell. Then how the month was worked out, line by line: days at the rate, each absence with its date and whether it was paid, what August owes him, what has been paid, what is still owed. Then the days themselves as chips you can add to or take away, which replaces the whole modal. Then the actions, with the accent on Pay — once, inside the one open row.

THE FIVE VERDICT BLOCKS BECOME ONE RAIL PANEL: "Needs a decision", three entries with dots and doors. The same facts, ~320px of coloured paragraph turned into ~150px of rail, off the path between the figures and the work. What was a fifth block — the days-missed tally — is a derived figure in the rail beside the rest.

HEIGHT: the two blocks above the list went from roughly 700px to 250px. The late rent and four people are on the first screen; previously the list had not started.

PAYING SOMEBODY →

This is the panel that replaces prompt() — and the second prompt that follows it asking which account. It opens inside the row, under the costing, so the month it is settling is on screen while you decide.

HOW MUCH, WITH THE TWO ANSWERS THAT ARE ALMOST ALWAYS RIGHT. The field is filled with the fortnight, because a shop paying twice a month pays half each time, and "the lot" is one tap away. Both figures are shown on the chips rather than named in a sentence, so nobody has to work out which is which. Anything else is typed.

THE ACCOUNT IS ASKED, AND ITS BALANCE IS ON THE CHOICE. Cash 640,000, mobile money 505,000, bank 305,000 — so you can see, at the moment of choosing, that this payment does not fit in the bank. A wage handed over in mobile money and logged against the drawer leaves both accounts wrong by the same amount and the day fails to reconcile with nothing on screen to say why. The current code asks the same question in a dialog; here it is three buttons with the answer already visible.

ONE LINE SAYS EXACTLY WHAT THE BUTTON WILL DO. What leaves, from where, filed under which Cash Book category, dated today, and what the month keeps owing afterwards — plus what it will NOT do: nothing is sent to anybody and nothing is told to her. Nothing sends itself is an app-wide law, and this is the screen where somebody might assume otherwise.

AND THE BUTTON SAYS IT TOO: "Pay 225,000 out of cash", not "Confirm".

SETTLED BEFORE THIS SYSTEM stays, as a quiet line rather than an option in a dialog: the month is closed and the Cash Book is left exactly as it stands. That is a bookkeeping act, not a payment, and it should not look like one.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DRAWN: reversing a payment. The row keeps its "Undo" and it still needs the same treatment — the current confirm() at least says whether a Cash Book entry will be removed, which is more than the payment path does.

← THE FOUR STATES

A — NOBODY IS ON THE PAYROLL YET. The screen says which of the two reasons applies: nobody has a pay rate, or nothing covers this month. It counts the people who ARE on the staff list, because "3 people, none with a rate" is a different sentence from "you have no staff", and only one of them is a thing to fix.

B — THE MONTH IS SETTLED. No strip of zeros: four tiles reading 0 makes a straight book look like a broken screen. One sentence, and the four figures worth keeping — what the month cost, split, and the days missed. That is the one reading of a settled payroll that is worth anything.

C — A PAST MONTH THAT WAS NEVER RAISED. This is the app's own scar: renderPayroll used to raise dues for whatever month was on screen, so paging back through the year wrote a wage for every worker into every month browsed, including months before the shop had hired them. A shop found eight million owed to people it had not yet employed, put there by reading. The button is the fix — but today it is an unexplained "Run this month's payroll" with no statement of what it will write. Here it says: nine months of liability, dated four months ago, at today's rates.

D — NO CASH FIGURE, SO NO COVER LINE. The tile reads "Not known" in amber — not 0 — and where the line would be, the screen says why it cannot be drawn and offers the door. Derived, never invented; a failure must name itself. Note the strip does NOT collapse: every other figure on the screen comes from the months themselves and needs no cash book, so paying still works. This matters practically — cbDayPosition() creates a day record as a side effect, so this screen must not call it merely to render, which is exactly why the figure can be genuinely absent.

All four are stacked here to compare the wording. In the app only one is ever on screen, so the accent still appears once.

THE PHONE — its own design, not the table reflowed

820px is a switch, so this is drawn from scratch at 390: 44px navy bar, 26px page name, 15px body, 14–16px row padding, 44px hit targets, and the docked action in the thumb zone.

THE PHONE JOB IS DIFFERENT. At the desk you are deciding who to pay out of what is in the drawer. In the yard, somebody did not come in — or a worker is asking what he is owed. So the strip still leads with the cash question, the cover line survives (turned into a full-bleed band, because a centred rule with text either side has no room at 390px), and the cards carry the reason line where it can be read at arm's length.

THE CARDS CARRY NO BUTTON, and the accent lives once, in the dock: RECORD A DAY SOMEBODY MISSED. That is your answer to the fourth question — read and record, do not pay — and it is also the honest one: an absence is dated and perishable, and the person who knows is the one standing in the yard. A payment can wait for the desk.

THE MONTH STEPPER IS 44px AND FULL WIDTH, because paging back a month on a phone is a thumb action, and the three ghost buttons the desktop screen uses today are 30px targets.

The list runs on under the dock, as a list does. No fake status bar, no fake keyboard.

ONE THING TO DECIDE: whether the phone should show what is still owed to each person at all, or only the month's position. I have drawn it showing figures, because a worker asking "how much am I owed" in the yard is exactly when you need it. If you would rather it were not readable over your shoulder, the cards can carry the reason line and hide the figure until tapped.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. THE RANKING RULE. Already late, then falls due soonest, then largest. "Largest first" within one day is my reading of the cash question — the big month is the one today's cash decides. If you would rather the person who has waited longest came first, or the daily workers who live on the money, it is one comparator.

2. WHERE THE RENT AGREEMENTS TABLE GOES. I have taken it off the screen and left a link in the rail, on the grounds that it is setup rather than work — you touch it when a tenancy starts or ends, twice a year. If you would rather it stayed visible, it comes back as a collapsed block under the queue, not as a panel with its own accent button.

3. "EARNED SO FAR" ON A RUNNING MONTH. The row shows 405,000 earned of a 450,000 salary on the 27th. It is what the balance sheet counts and what somebody paid by the fortnight actually asks for. It is also a second figure on a row that already has one, and you may find it noise on a screen where you pay the whole month anyway.

4. THE OVERPAYMENT. I have left it as a decision in the rail, not an action — the app takes nothing back on its own. If you want "take it off next month" to be a button, that is a real feature and a real decision about somebody's pay, and it needs its own drawing.

5. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED: the days-missed modal is replaced on the desktop by the chips inside the open row, but the phone still needs a sheet drawn for it. The rent agreement form, the reversal confirm(), and the printed sheet are all untouched.
